[^70]: Search according to the content given at the beginning of the Psalter. The Psalter is divided into three parts, of which the first covers all weeks from the Sunday of Thomas the Apostle to Great Lent, the second -- Great Lent, the third -- Passion Week. In Bright Week the Psalter is not read.
[^71]: Since the *Octoechos* gives 6 stichera, and the Typikon does not determine which 3 of the 6 to take, we leave this to the judgment of the Reader. However, to say how it is better, let us first recall that the daily service of the *Octoechos* is double, that is: on Monday -- Penitential and to the Bodiless [Powers], on Tuesday -- Penitential and to the Forerunner, on Wednesday and Friday -- to the Cross and the Theotokos, on Thursday -- to the Apostles and Nicholas, on Saturday -- to all Saints and the Departed. Thus, in order not to discard either of the two services of the weekday, the Greek *Octoechos* (Παρακλητική /Parakletike/), printed in the "Propaganda" in 1738, gives from the three stichera of the first service only the two first stichera, and from the three stichera of the second service -- only one, the first. Among us, so that the printed stichera given in the *Octoechos* do not remain in vain, it would be possible to sing alternating all three stichera of the first service and all three stichera of the second service, that is, one year, odd -- three of the first service, and the second year, even -- three of the second service, or, even better -- one year two first stichera of the first service and one sticheron, the first, of the second service, and the second year -- one sticheron, the third, of the first service and two last of the second service. The Greek Typikon takes nothing from the *Octoechos*, but only three stichera from the *Menaion* on 6, repeating each (Καιφ. ε /chapter 5/). The Moscow Typikon takes three first stichera of the Theotokos from the *Octoechos*, which do not exist in our editions, but we find them in the Greek-Venetian edition; the Moscow *Octoechos* of 1782 has the same stichera as ours.
[^72]: In the Greek Menaion after the Doxastikon to the saint his Theotokion is also added. If there is no Doxastikon, then only certain most general Theotokia of the *Octoechos* are indicated by initial words; it is implied that they are known, although the number of *Octoechos* editions makes their search inconvenient. We cite here some: 1. Θεοτόκε, συ ει ο άμπελος "O Theotokos, Thou Art the vine" (Venetian *Octoechos*, Tone 6, on the Aposticha); θεον σαρκοΰεντα εκ σου "God incarnate from Thee" (Tone 6, on Saturday, Praises, Moscow edition); Δέσποινα προσδεξαι "O Sovereign Lady, receive" (Tone 8, on Saturday at Matins; Την πασαν ελπίδα "All my hope" (Tone 2, on Thursday, on the Aposticha of Matins). Sometimes the Theotokion is not indicated even by initial words, but is only named generally: θεοτοκιον ομοιον /Theotokion similar/, or only: θεοτοκιον /Theotokion/ (Menaion September 3, August 2); in this case one must select a Theotokion from the *Octoechos*. Four aforementioned Theotokia are given also on *“Lord, I have cried”*, and on the Aposticha (Menaion November 1 and 3, December 5, July 1). In the last edition of the Venetian Menaion Theotokia are given almost always fully. But among us, at the end of every volume of the Menaion are given all Theotokia that are taken on *“Lord, I have cried”* and on the Aposticha, and not only for every tone, but also for every day of the week, in order not to repeat the same Theotokia many times. In the Pochaiv *Anthologion* Theotokia are given only according to the tone, and not also according to the day; and in general services sometimes only the first words are cited, and they themselves are not given.

Regarding small litanies which are read between kathismata and sessional hymns, the Lviv Synod, our Horologions and our Sluzhebnyky (at the end) give them also at Small Matins, and they are used also by the Greek-Melkites (according to the testimony of their patriarch bl. m. Clement Bahous). Conversely, in the Russian Typikon, approved by their Governing Synod (Moscow edition of 1859), in the Order of Daily Matins it is written that the Priest says them only at the Vigil and when the memory of saints having a Polyeleos and Doxology is celebrated; similarly also in the new Wallachian-Bucharest Typikon, in which in the Order of Daily Matins is given: "We take sessional hymns from the *Octoechos* without litanies" (untranslatable); and adds: "In monasteries, usually, between kathismata litanies are taken only on Sunday and when more special saints occur". From the Greek Typikon no conclusion can be made, for in it small litanies are not mentioned neither at Small Matins, nor at Great, nor before the Canon, nor after the Canon. It is assumed in the Typikon that this is known to everyone. From the rubrics of the Greek *Triodion*, given at Matins on Meatfare Saturday, one can conclude that these litanies should be said also at Small Matins. For it gives: η συνηιϊης στιχολογια. Εν δε ταις συναπταις πασαις της στιχολογιας και του Κανόνος, μνημονεύονται πάντες οι προαπελΰοντες Πατέρες και αδελφοί ημων /Ordinary Stichology. In all small litanies of the Stichology and of the Canon, all our fathers and brethren who have passed away before us are commemorated/. Let everyone observe the rubric and custom of his Church. Finally, in our opinion, later typikons reject litanies here only for the sake of greater shortening of the divine service; if the single difference between Small and Great Matins were the rejection or use of litanies, then this difference should have been indicated in some place of ancient liturgical books; however, this is not encountered. What the exclamation of the third litany should be is not indicated in any of the church books. Therefore we are forced to borrow it from Great Matins. At Great Matins in Slavonic books two exclamations are given which are used at the third litany, that is one -- for Sunday "For blessed is" and the second -- for Polyeleos feasts "For holy Art Thou". For the sake of distinguishing the Sunday day from the ordinary day, at Small Matins it is appropriate to use the second "For holy Art Thou", although it would not be bad to use also the first "For blessed is" (Οτι ευλογητοα), for in Greek books we find only this one exclamation, without distinction of day. Regarding Sessional Hymns, they are taken two or three after each stichology, depending on the edition, except the Theotokion. In Lviv editions of the *Octoechos* and in the Greek-Venetian one, only to the Theotokion is sung "Glory, Both now". In the Pochaiv and Moscow ones a separate refrain is also given to every second, or even to the third sessional hymn. This refrain, corresponding to the content of the sessional hymn: on Monday and Tuesday -- Penitential "O Lord, rebuke me not in Thine anger"; on Wednesday and Friday -- of the Cross, and on Thursday -- of the Apostles; to the third sessional hymn, that is the Martyron -- also the Martyron refrain: "Wondrous is God in His saints".

[^91]: The Greek Typikon gives the whole service only to the saint, and Apostle and Gospel -- first of the day, and then of the saint; Προκειμενον του κατά την ημεραν Αγιου, Αλληλούια του Αγιου, Ευαγγελιον της ημέρας και του Αγιου. (Καιφ. σ) /Prokimenon of the saint of the day, Alleluia of the saint, Gospel of the day and of the saint (chapter 6)/. So also in chapter 99, Mark. Although this rubric is given only in the Saturday service, however, it must be understood that also on other days of the week it should be so. Slavonic typikons prescribe the whole service to the day and to the saint, if he has one, and troparia -- also to the temple, if it is of the Lord or of the Theotokos. The Moscow Typikon also prescribes to the temple, if the temple is of a saint (although this does not agree with the rubric of that same Typikon, given on September 26 and January 30); this same Typikon ends the Kontakia with the Kontakion for the Dead *“With the saints give rest”* with the refrain "Glory" and the Kontakion of the temple, if it is of the Lord or of the Theotokos, if -- not, then with the usual "Protection" ("O Undisputed Intercessor") with the refrain "Both now" (chapter 52). This custom we find also among Greek-Italians and Greek-Melkites, but it does not exist among Constantinopolitan Greeks and Athonites, with the exception of some. But, since according to the rubric of the Greek Typikon, two Apostles and two Gospels were to be taken, and according to the Slavonic rubric, also the whole service of the day and of the saint, if he has one, and, since many saints (over one hundred eighty) have an Apostle and Gospel, as follows from the content of the Apostle-Gospel, therefore, in order to shorten the duration of the divine service, followers of the Greek Rite began already many years ago to reject certain rubrics; therefore also our Ruthenians take at the Liturgy only the service of the day, and reject the saint without Polyeleos; some -- conversely: take only the service to the saint, and reject the service of the day, as evidenced by the Pochaiv *Sluzhebnik* of 1765, which gives the Apostle and Gospel only on Sundays, and on weekdays -- only in Bright Week and in the week after the Descent of the Holy Spirit, similarly as Latin Missals, which give the Apostle and Gospel of the day only in these two mentioned weeks, for Great Lent and for certain other days. This custom we find also among Greek-Italians, observed also by some of those who are called Orthodox, whom the Moscow Typikon accuses, saying: "The Ecumenical Church does not take neither on the Beatitudes, nor at Liturgies the Apostle and Gospel to the saint on every day, only the sequential, that is the pillar throughout the whole year, in sequence, as also of selected saints who have an Apostle and Gospel. And if the Apostle and Gospel of the saint is read every day, then this is from one's own ignorance, and not according to the church typikon" (chapter 58, at the end). Exactly so also in the manuscript of the three-hundred-year-old Gospel that is among us. However, this rubric of the Ecumenical Church is not observed by the Constantinopolitan Hierarch, called Ecumenical, nor by the Churches subject to him, who (according to the testimony of hierarch Benjamin Νεαπολεος /of Neapolis/, who lived in Constantinople and on Mount Athos, who in our times accepted church union) have the custom, also in monasteries, to take the Apostle and Gospel only of the day, if the saint does not have one, if he has, then only to the saint, and in another they adhere to the new Constantinopolitan Typikon, printed in the patriarchal typography in 1851, marked with the patriarchal seal and confirmed by signatures of all patriarchs and hierarchs subject to them. In this Typikon there, where the rubric gives two Apostles and Gospels, one Apostle-Gospel is given, that is the Apostle -- of the first service, and the Gospel -- of the second service. Thus e. g. October 26, November 21, when they fall on a Sunday and on John the Theologian May 8, when it falls on Ascension.

[^197]: About the commemoration of the feast at the Dismissal in the Afterfeast we find nothing in Greek typikons. From the Typikon of Slavonic Triodia and of the Moscow Typikon one could conclude that the commemoration of the feast should be taken only on the very solemn day of the feast and on its Apodosis. For it prescribes to take the Paschal Dismissal throughout the whole Bright Week, every day of which has the form of the divine service of the very day of the Resurrection, and afterwards prescribes to take it at the Liturgy of the Apodosis of the Resurrection. However, today we observe the general custom to make the festal commemoration also on other days of the Afterfeast, which has also the rubric of the *Sluzhebnik*, printed in Stratyn under the Lviv Bishop Gedeon Balaban in 1604, 11 years before the *Tserkovne Oko*, which gives the following: "Know, that festal dismissals are taken from the day of the feast until the Apodosis of the feast of every day" (page 517). Similarly one could take in Theotokion Afterfeasts, but the words "today" and "solemnly" must be discarded. However, in Afterfeasts of the Lord it is better not to take the commemoration of the feast on Sunday, for it does not combine well with the Sunday commemoration, which must occupy the first place. It would be, e. g. on the Afterfeast of the Nativity of Christ: "Who rose from the dead and Who was born in a cavern in Bethlehem of Judea and let Himself be laid in a manger for our salvation, Christ, our true God". And on weekdays, except Sunday, the commemoration of the feast can be taken without doubt, for then the service of the feast replaces the service of the *Octoechos* and therefore, instead of the commemoration of the service of the day, that is of the *Octoechos*, it is good to take the commemoration of the service of the feast. Some on Sunday discard the Sunday commemoration and take only of the feast, but they act contrary to our Sluzhebnyky, which on the Sunday of the Holy Fathers, in the middle of the feast of the Ascension before Pentecost, give the Sunday commemoration.

[^201]: According to the most general and most ancient typikons in the Afterfeast and on the Apodosis the Trisagion should be taken, and not "As many as have been baptized into Christ" or "Before Thy Cross", for they are taken on the very day of the feast, with the exception of "As many as have been baptized into Christ", which is taken not only on the very day of the Resurrection, but also throughout the whole Bright Week, since throughout the whole Bright Week the divine service takes place as on the very day of the Resurrection. On other days, until the Apodosis of the Resurrection, the Trisagion is taken. So have the general Greek and Slavonic typikons and the most ancient Typikon of the Monastery of St. Nicholas of Casole in the district of Otranto, kept in the Barberini library in Rome, written six hundred or seven hundred years ago. In it on fol. 121 and 124 is given the Typikon, which I gave. With this general and ancient typikon one Greek Typikon does not agree, written by the Reverend Father Bartholomew, a companion of the Reverend Father Nilus and co-founder of the Monastery of Grottaferrata near Rome, kept in that same monastery, which prescribes "As many as have been baptized into Christ" until the Apodosis of the feast. E. g. December 26 gives: Και αντί του Τρισάγιου Οσοι εις Χριστον. Τούτο γαρ λεγομεν έως ου αποδιδοται η εορτή /And instead of the Trisagion As many as have been baptized into Christ. For this we say until the feast is taken leave of/. Does not agree also the new Constantinopolitan Typikon 1851, marked with the seal of the Patriarch. See, e. g. on Monday of the Holy Spirit there, where Greek and Slavonic Triodia have the Trisagion, this Typikon has "As many as have been baptized into Christ". Regarding Troparia, Mark thus: Sunday, Glory: Troparion to the saint, if he has, Both now: Kontakion of the feast (Καιφ. ξε)/chapter 65/.

(14 September). The beginning is usual and other preparatory prayers, that is Trisagion with "Our Father", as later Slavic typikons give, longer than this entire order, for it consists only of one Troparion of the Cross, and with the Slavic addition, also of a Kontakion.
[^264]: Ancient Greek typikons mention nothing about a Deacon, neither at the bringing out, nor at the exaltation, nor at the laying of the precious Cross, but only about one priest. The Greek typikon, similarly to the Slavic ones, prescribes for the Priest to vest in all priestly vestments: αλασσει ο Ιερεύς πασαν την ιερατικην στολην /the Priest vests in all priestly vestments/. The Greek *Triodion* (Sunday of the Veneration of the Cross) and the new Constantinopolitan Typikon, similarly to Slavic typikons, prescribes for the Priest to enter with the cross from the sanctuary to the temple through the northern doors: εκ του αριστερού Βήματος /from the left side of the sanctuary/. Greek typikons, with the exception of the new Constantinopolitan, and the Slavic of the Lviv University, prescribe for the Priest, having exited from the sanctuary to the temple, to head to the entrance doors that lead from the temple to the narthex, which are sometimes called royal, and there await the end of the Doxology and from there exclaim "Wisdom, attend", and then head to the tetrapod, which is before the iconostasis. Although these doors are called royal, βασιλικαι /royal/, one must understand that they were called so in the past. Today we call royal the middle doors of the iconostasis, which according to ancient custom are called holy: αγιαι ΰυραι /holy doors/ (chapter 96, Greek Typikon).

And the censer, which with us the Priest holds with the cross, it would be better for the Deacon to hold and cense, as the new Constantinopolitan Typikon and the *Tserkovne Oko* prescribe on 14 September.

According to general Slavic typikons: to the east, to the west, to the south, to the north and again to the east. According to the Greek Typikon: to the east, to the south, to the west, to the north and again to the east. The new Constantinopolitan Typikon prescribes as with us.

From this it follows that they had particles of the precious Cross in monasteries. The Greek Typikon and two handwritten Slavic ones that you have, do not prescribe for the Priest to sing separately "Before Thy Cross", but for the choirs; nor to bow to the precious Cross to the ground; for only the *Tserkovne Oko* prescribes this on 14 September.

Also the Greek Typikon, having discarded both last litanies, immediately after the veneration gives the dismissal: Ψαλλομενης δε της μεγάλης δοξολογίας, αλασσει ο Ιερεύς πασαν την ιερατικην στολην, και εισέρχεται μετά του θυμιατού, προηγουμένων των λαμπάδων, εν τη αγία Τρεπεζη, και Ουμιων τον αγιον σταυρόν σταυροειδως, αίρει αυτόν μετά δίσκου επί καιφαλης, και προπορευόμενων δυο λαμπάδων, φέρει αυτόν μέχρι των βασιλικών πυλών του ναού, κακεισαι ισταται. Και πληρουμενης της δοξολογίας και του τρισάγιου, λέγει ο Ιερεύς μεγαλόφωνος: Σοφια ορθοί. Και αρχόμενα του τροπαρίου Σωσον Κύριε, και ούτως εισοδευει μετά του αγίου σταυρού, και ούτως ευτρεπισμενου τετραποδιου, τνθεται ο τίμιος σταυρός επάνω αυτού, και Ουμια ο Ιερεύς σταυροειδως. ЕІ6 ούτως βολών μετανοίας τρεις, καν ποια εστίν ήμερα, και λαβών ανά χείρας τον τιμιον σταυρόν γυμνον μετά βασιλικών κλάδων, ισταται έμπροσθεν του τετραποδιου, βλέπων κατ ανατολάς, και λέγει εις επηκοον πάντων: Ελεησον ημάς ο Θεός. Και αρχόμενα της πρώτης εκατοντάδας το Κύριε ελεησον, σφραγίζοντας του Ιερέως εν ταις εναρξεσιν μετά του αγίου σταυρού. Είτα κλίνει την καιφαλην όσον σπιύαμην από της γης, και καταμικρον ανισταται άχρι συμπληρωσεος της εκατοντάδας. Ηνικα δε φθάσει ενς το 97 Κύριε ελεησον, υψοι την φωνην ο Εκκλησιαρχης, ήγουν το Κύριε ελεησον τρις, και αισθομενος ο Ιερεύς τέλος λαμβάνειν την εκατοντάδα, σφραγίζει πάλιν τρις. Είτα στραφείς επί το νοτιον μέρος, λέγει: Ετι δεομεβα... και αρχόμενα της δευτέρας εκατοντάδας, και ποιεί ο Ιερεύς την δεύτερον υψωσιν, ως προγεγραπται. Ειύ ούτως στραφείς επί δυσμάς λέγει: Ετι δεομεθα, και αρχόμενα της τρίτης εκατοντάδας. Πληρωμένης δε αυτής, στρέφεται ο Ιερεύς επί το βορειον μέρος, και λέγει: Ετι δεομεθα... και γίνεται η τετάρτη υψωσις. Και ούτως στρέφεται ο Ιερεύς κατ ανατολάς, και λέγει: Ετι δεομεύα... και αρχομεΟα της πέμπτης εκατοντάδας. Μετά δε την πεμπτην υψωσιν ψαλλομεν το Κοντακιον Ο υψωθείς. ЕІІ9 ούτως: Τον σταυρόν σου προσκυνουμεν Δέσποτα τρεις. Ψαλλόντων δε των αδελφών, αποτι6ισιν ο Ιερεύς το τιμιον ξυλον εν τετραποδιω, και αρχόμενα προσκυνειν, ο τε Ιερεύς, και ο Προεστως, ποιουντες και μετανοίας τρεις κατενωπιον του τυμιου σταυρού, είτα ασπάζονται. Και μετά το ασπαζαστ)αι βαλλουσιν μιαν μετανοιαν; ειΰ ούτως εις τους χορούς δεξιά και αριστερά. Είτα εισέρχονται οι αδελφοί δυο δυο κατά ταξιν, και προσκυνουσι και ασπάζονται ομοίως. Ψαλλομεν δε και τα στιχηρα ιδιομελα, αχρις ουν προσκυνουσιν οι αδελφοί, εις ηχον β το Δεύτε πιστοί. Και μετά το προσκυνησαι παντός λέγει ο Ιερεύς: Σοφια, και Απολυσις /During the singing of the Great Doxology the Priest vests in all priestly vestments and proceeds with the censer, preceded by candle-bearers, to the holy table. Having censed the holy cross crosswise, he takes it with the diskos on his head and, preceded by two candle-bearers, carries it to the royal doors of the temple, remaining there. At the end of the Doxology and Trisagion, the Priest loudly exclaims: "Wisdom, attend!" and we begin the troparion "Save, O Lord". The Priest enters with the holy cross and places the precious cross on the prepared tetrapod, having censed it crosswise. Then, having bowed three times, whatever day it may be, he takes into his hands the precious cross, wrapped with basil branches, stands before the tetrapod, looking to the east, and says so that all can hear: "Have mercy on us, O God". And we begin "Lord, have mercy" of the first hundred, and the Priest at the beginning blesses with the holy cross. After this he bows his head to, approximately, a quarter of a meter from the ground and gradually rises until the end of the hundred. When "Lord, have mercy" is sung for the 97th time, the Ecclesiarch raises his voice. Then "Lord, have mercy" is sung three times, and the Priest, noticing that the hundred is coming to an end, again signs three times with the cross. Then he, having turned to the south, says: "Again we pray" and we begin the second hundred, and the Priest performs the second exaltation of the cross, as prescribed. Then, turned to the west, says: "Again we pray" and we begin the third hundred. At the end, the Priest turns to the north and says: "Again we pray" and the fourth exaltation takes place. Then the Priest turns to the east and says: "Again we pray" and we begin the fifth hundred. After the fifth exaltation we sing the Kontakion "Thou Who Wast lifted up" ("Voznesyisya"). Then "Before Thy Cross" is sung three times. While the brethren sing, the Priest places the precious cross on the tetrapod and we begin to venerate. The Priest and the Superior, having bowed three times before the precious cross, kiss it. After kissing they bow once. Also those in the choirs on the right and left. Then the brethren approach two by two, according to rank, bowing, simultaneously and kiss. We sing the stichera idiomesa, while the brethren venerate, in Tone 2 "Come, ye faithful". And when all have finished venerating, the Priest exclaims: "Wisdom!" and the dismissal follows/ (14 September).

But our liturgikons, horologia and the Greek-Venetian *Menaion* of 1755 prescribe to take the Service of the Holy Fathers on the Sunday following 11 October; one must understand, that when 11 October falls on a weekday; similarly in the latest Greek-Venetian *Menaion* (1884) and in the new Constantinopolitan Typikon, where it is prescribed to take on the very day of 11 October, if Sunday, if -- not, then on the following Sunday. What shall we say to this? We consider that all these rules are good, however, it is not good when liturgical books of one and the same church province give uncoordinated rules. For when we accept the rule of our *Menaion*, then let it be placed also in the liturgikons And in the horologia, for when we accept the rule of the latter, then let It be also in the *Menaion*. And if we adhere to the rule of the *Menaion*, then it is necessary to present it already on 8 October, so that, reading, one can notice about the Following Sunday. This must be understood also about the Service of the Holy Fathers of the First Six Councils on 16 July, which the menaia both ours and Greek, Prescribe to transfer back, to 13 July, if it falls on Wednesday; the Greek menaia present this not in accordance with their rule on 11 October, when they prescribe to transfer this service from 16 July back, they have to transfer it back also from 11 October. It seems to us, And it would be simpler not to transfer these services back, but to take on the very [days of] 11 October and 16 July, when they fall on Sunday, if -- not, on the following Sunday.

In the new Constantinopolitan -- Troparia of the Earthquake, and everything else -- only to the Saint. According to the general Slavic typikon, which is adhered to only in cathedral churches, before the Apostle-Gospel of the Saint, the Apostle-Gospel also of the day is taken.

[^275]: According to the rule of our *Menaion*, Moscow Typikon and *Tserkovne Oko* -- / Resurrectional Troparion, of the Earthquake and of the Saint. Resurrectional Kontakion, Glory: to the Saint, Both now: of the Earthquake. Everything else -- to the Earthquake, and afterwards -- to the Saint; Apostle-Gospel -- sequential, under the Prokimenon (zaspiv). The Greek *Menaion* of 1755 gives nothing of the Earthquake.

[^277]: Some consider, according to the edition of the Peremyshl Typikon of 1870, p. 271, that neither on St. Michael, nor on St. Prophet Elias, should *“Blessed is the man”* be sung and, that then not a single kathisma is taken, for this kathisma, as the publisher writes about it, is found only in the Pochaiv Anthologion, and in the most ancient menaia and Anthologia they are not mentioned; the reason for this is considered to be that "Elias did not die, and St. Michael, as bodiless, is not subject to death". However, this is not enough. For regarding the rule, not only the Pochaiv Anthologion (Anthologion) of 1777 and the Pochaiv *Menaion* of the same year, but also the Lviv Anthologion (Anthologion) of 1643 and the Great Typikon, under the title *Tserkovne Oko*, printed in Moscow in 1615, that is more than a century and a half before the Pochaiv Anthologion, and the manuscript Anthologion of 1736, which we have, and the Typikon of the All-Russian Church, printed in Moscow in 1859, by the decision of its Governing Synod, give also on these two feasts the kathisma *“Blessed is the man”*. Although some rules, like the Moscow *Menaion* of 1782, the Greek-Venetian of 1884 do not give *“Blessed is the man”*, it does not follow from this that no kathisma is needed, for even on Saints without Polyeleos in the *Menaion* a kathisma is not given, but the sequential one is meant; so here one can understand the sequential one, which three ancient handwritten Slavic typikons give: one -- of the Lviv University, the second -- of St. Onuphrius in Lviv, and the third -- of the library of the Chapter of St. George; also *Tserkovne Oko* (which gives two rules: one with *“Blessed is the man”*, and the second with the sequential kathisma). The reason that these rules give for these two feasts a sequential kathisma, may lie in the fact that their service initially had neither All-Night Vigil nor Polyeleos, but gradually, with time, grew into All-Night Vigil. About St. Elias it is written in the Pochaiv *Menaion*: "Let it be known that in printed Greek menaia, in handwritten typikons, and also in Slavic handwritten and printed typikons, the service of the Prophet Elias is given on 6, with *Octoechos*". And regarding St. Michael, the above-mentioned Slavic typikons give him a service only of the Polyeleos type, but incomplete, for they partially combine his service with the service of the *Octoechos*, as for a Saint without Polyeleos.

Decrees of the Sacred Congregation of Indulgences of 22 March 1847, about the pious order of St. Joseph the Betrothed.
[^279]: We find the Service of St. Catherine as having Polyeleos only in our Pochaiv *Menaion* and in the new Greek-Venetian one; but in others -- without Polyeleos. In later Greek typikons we find it given on 25 November with the Apodosis of the Feast of the Entry into the Temple of the Most Holy Theotokos, and in earlier ones -- on the 24th, as it is today among Greek-Slavs. Thus the Greek-Venetian *Menaion* of 1615 gives: Σημειωσαι ουν, ότι ευρομεν εν τισι Τυπικοις των νεωτέρων, ότι εν τιοα των πόλεων ψαλλεται η ακολουθία της αγίας μάρτυρος Αικατερίνης εν τη κε του μηνός, εν η και αποδιδοται η εορτή. Εν ετεροις δε Τυπικοις παλαιοτεροις ευρομεν αυτήν εορτάζεσαι εν τη κδ του αυτού μηνός: εν δε τη κε ψαλλομεν την ακολουθίαν του εν αγιοις Κλημεντος Παπα Ρώμης, και Πέτρου Αλεξανδρείας, εν η και αποδιδοται η εορτή των Εισοδιων /Note, therefore, that we found in some newer typikons, that in some places the service of the holy martyr Catherine is sung on the 25th day of this month, on which the feast is also given up. In other older typikons we found that her memory is celebrated on the 24th of this month, and on the 25th we sing the service of Saints Clement Pope of Rome and Peter of Alexandria, and on this day also the feast of the Entry is given up/. This transfer from the 24th to the 25th day, in the opinion of the Greeks, as explained by the new Greek-Venetian *Menaion* (24 November, p. 158), was done at the wish of the monks of Mount Sinai, so that it would not coincide with the Apodosis of the feast and, so that in this way the memory of the saint would be honored more solemnly. For we know that the body of the holy great martyr was transferred by angelic power to Mount Sinai and buried there.

Russian typikons prescribe to take this stichera once without a refrain, which the canonarch or Deacon reads, adding the Many Years to the Emperor, in Constantinople: λέγει το εγκωμιον του Πατριάρχου/reads the encomium of the Patriarch/. [^337]: Greek menaia and typikons give a rule only for two cases of Saturdays and Sundays between the Nativity and Theophany, that is: one -- for two Saturdays and two Sundays; the second -- for one Saturday and one Sunday, and for these one Saturday and one Sunday they give the following rule: Ει δε τύχη εν Σαββατον και μια Κυριακή, αναγινωσκεται τω μεν Σαββατω, Σαββατω μετά την Χρίστου γεννησιν, τη δε Κυριακή, Κυριακή προ των Φοτων /If there should happen to be one Saturday and one Sunday, on the Saturday is read that which is also on the Saturday after the Nativity of Christ, and on the Sunday that which is on the Sunday before Theophany/. And this rule is enough for the case of one Saturday with one Sunday, for then this Saturday falls during December (the 31st), and the Sunday -- during January (the 1st); however, it is not enough for one Saturday with two Sundays, nor for one Sunday with two Saturdays, for then this Saturday falls during January (the 1st), as in the seventh row, and the Sunday -- during December (the 31st), as this is in the 3rd row; and as it is not possible, according to the Greek Typikon itself, to read the Apostle-Gospel of the Sunday after the Nativity outside the feast of the Nativity, in January, but it must be transferred back, to 26 December δια το αρχήν λαμβάνειν τον Ιαννουαριον μήνα, και την των Χρίστου Γεννών εορτην αποδιδοσΟαι /because the month of January begins and the feast of the Nativity of Christ is given up/: so it is not possible to read the Apostle-Gospel of the Sunday before Theophany, within the feast of the Nativity, or the Apostle-Gospel of the Saturday after the Nativity to read in January. Therefore there is nothing strange that the Slavs supplemented their rules with what was lacking. However, the rules of our *Menaion* and the Russian ones, given on 26 December, for Saturdays and Sundays between the Nativity and Theophany, likely due to the negligence of copyists, in some places gave incorrectly and must be corrected, in our opinion, thus: The rule of the first case: "If the Nativity falls on a Sunday", then it should end thus: "as in the present section in the row it will appear, if the Circumcision and Basil fall on a Sunday" (as in the following case). The rule of the third case, "if the Nativity on Tuesday", then from the words: "And on Sunday" to the end, and should be: "And on Sunday, which is before Theophany, Prokimenon, Apostle, Alleluia and Gospel we read on the first day of January, as will be in the row, if the Circumcision and Basil fall on a Sunday". The rule of the fifth case from the words: "And on the second day Prokimenon, Apostle, Alleluia and Gospel we read first of the Sunday before Theophany, and then -- of the Saint" and everything that is there. The rule prescribes to read in this case at Matins two Gospels: one of the Sunday, and the second -- sequential, we do not know from where it has this, for besides one sequential Sunday Gospel at Matins we know not, because the Sunday before Theophany has nothing at Matins.

All sing the troparion many times, until all the brethren are sanctified by the sprinkling with water and kissing". The *Menaion* prescribes also to the Saint, if he has something, according to the rule given before for the Synaxis of the Forerunner here on [p. 201](Final_Dolnytsky_part3_menaion.md#7-january--synaxis-of-the-holy-glorious-prophet-forerunner-and-baptist-john); however, for a Saint without Polyeleos now with us nothing is taken. However, with us now the custom is adhered to of celebrating the Service of the Presanctified only on Wednesdays and Fridays, and on the other three fast days -- the Service of Chrysostom, after which, in cathedral churches, the three last Hours with the Typika are also sung, and Vespers -- at 11 o'clock. Regarding the litanies, our and Russian typikons mention litanies after the 3rd kathisma, from this it follows that after the 1st and 2nd kathismata there are no litanies, which the Pochaiv *Triodion* also excludes after the 1st kathisma before the sessional hymn of the *Triodion* on 25 March; and assuming such, it is proper to take two small litanies: one -- before the post-Polyeleos sessional hymn, with the exclamation "For blessed is Thy name", and the second -- before the sessional hymn of the 3rd kathisma, with the exclamation "For Thou Art good" or "For Thine is the dominion", at choice. Since in reality we do not serve a Panakhida today after Vespers, we say its litanies at least at Vespers and at Matins; although our Horologia (at the end) provide the litany for the dead "Have mercy on us, O God" only at the end of Matins. After the dismissal of this [service], we add also "In blessed falling asleep" just as at the Parastas. At Matins we say the small litanies in their places, that is, after the Kathisma and in the Canon, after Odes 3, 6, and 9; we say the usual ones, and not for the dead, since our Pochaiv *Triodion* does not prescribe litanies for the dead at that time. *Tserkovne Oko* and the Moscow Typikon prescribe the litany for the dead after Ode 6. The Greek *Triodion* prescribes commemorating the dead at the litany after the Kathisma and at all litanies of the Canon: "At all litanies of the Stichology and of the Canon, all our departed fathers and brethren are commemorated". Our Manuscript Typikon agrees with this, in which: the Priest pronounces the petitions; either after the Kathisma or after the Canon he always mentions the dead. The *Euchologion* of Benedict XIV on the litany for the dead gives the prayer only when it begins with "Have mercy on us, O God", and never if it begins with "Again and again".
[^471]: Exactly so both our Manuscript Typikon and *Tserkovne Oko* prescribe: "and the verses – of Vespers". The usual verses given in the *Horologion* for "Alleluia" after *“God is the Lord”* are sometimes read on Saturdays throughout the year on which a saint has a service but does not have a troparion.

[^555]: The Order of the Akathist, that is the Non-Sitting [Hymn], is sung in memory of the triple deliverance of Constantinople from the invasion of enemies, thanks to the intercession of the Mother of God, whose precious robe, brought from Jerusalem and placed by St. Pulcheria in the Blachernae church, and the Icon of the Hodegetria, painted, in the opinion of the Greeks, by St. Luke, were carried around the city, invoking her help. The first invasion was under Emperor Heraclius (reigned from 610 to 641) from the Persian army, led by the satrap Sarvar, and also from the Scythian army, under the command of the Khagan. Part of the enemies were destroyed by a small number of armed Christians who came out of the temple of the Most Holy Theotokos, and partly -- by a strong sea storm which destroyed their ships. The second invasion was 36 years later, that is under Constantine Pogonatos (668-685) and ended partly by the disease of the soldiers, and partly -- by a sea storm when they were returning home. The third was under Leo the Isaurian (717-741) and ended by a sea storm, famine, division of forces against the Bulgarians, by whom they were beaten (Synaxarion of this Saturday, about which also Nilles, Calend. vol. 2, p. 152).
[^556]: Besides the initial Kontakion "To the Directress", the rest of the Akathist consists of 12 Ikos and 12 Kontakia, together -- of 24 members according to the number of 24 letters of the Greek alphabet, with which each member, in the Greek text, begins in sequence.
[^557]: In the Patriarchal Church of Constantinople the Akathist is sung not at Matins, but before that, at Small Compline, that is at *“It is truly meet”* -- the first station by the Patriarch himself, the second -- after the 3rd Ode of the canon of the feast by the Bishop of Caesarea, the third -- after the 6th Ode by the Bishop of Ephesus, the fourth -- after the 9th Ode by the Bishop of Heraclea (New Constantinopolitan Typikon).
[^558]: The Greek *Triodion* does not prescribe any censing. *Tserkovne Oko* and our Manuscript Typikon prescribe 4 censings, as do ours and the Russian rubrics, however, they order to cense only the icons and the brethren, ours and the Russian -- only the icons and the brethren, and at the other three stations -- only the Superior and the choirs. It would be better for us to cense only once, at the beginning.

Where date palms do not grow, there only olive branches are used; and among us, since olives also do not grow, willow branches are used, hence also in *Tserkovne Oko*: "reciting the prayer over the willow".

[^588]: In Greek rubrics and in one Slavonic manuscript *Triodion* which we have, neither censing at any of the 12 Gospels, nor Small Litany is prescribed. *Tserkovne Oko* prescribes a Small Litany both at the first Gospel and before all five Sessional Hymns, and prescribes leaving the censing at the 8th, 9th, 10th and 11th Gospels. The new Constantinopolitan Typikon prescribes one censing not at the Gospel, but at the beginning of Matins, during the Two Psalms according to the general rubric of Matins. But since among us at Small Matins this censing is omitted, at least here we have given at the first [Gospel] -- censing not only of the holy table, but also of the icons, and choirs, according to the general rubric of the beginning of Matins. Although Greek rubrics at these Gospels do not prescribe censing, nothing strange, for in Greek and Slavonic Typika at Matins Gospels censing is not prescribed. *Tserkovne Oko* prescribes at the first Gospel two censings: one -- at the beginning, only of the holy table and the whole sanctuary, the second -- at the end: of the whole church, images and choirs. At the six following -- censing of images, the Superior and choirs (however, here it inconsistently agrees with itself, when it is given that at the Sessional Hymns the Priest or deacon censes also the holy table); at Gospels 8, 9, 10 and 11 it does not prescribe censing, and at the 12th again prescribes censing of the whole church, choirs and brethren. The Moscow Typikon follows *Tserkovne Oko*, however, at the 1st Gospel prescribes only one censing, at the beginning -- of the whole temple; it prescribes inaccurately that the litanies of the Sessional Hymns are said up to the 8th Gospel, for the Sessional Hymns extend only to the 6th Gospel. Although Greek rubrics do not prescribe censing at the Gospels, nevertheless, at the Sessional Hymns they prescribe standing. "We do not sit at such Sessional Hymns, but we sing them standing".
[^589]: In the Patriarchate of Constantinople the first -- the Patriarch, the twelfth -- the Grand Archdeacon from the ambo; and at the beginning, at the Two Psalms, censes the Grand Archimandrite, dressed in a golden phelonion (New Constantinopolitan Typikon).
[^590]: Today it is sufficient to sing once.
[^591]: *Tserkovne Oko* prescribes repeating also the Theotokion, however, since the Theotokion serves to end the troparia, it should not be repeated; in the *Triodion* the refrain "Glory, Both now" is given together before the Theotokion.
[^592]: The Moscow Typikon prescribes 9, it must be understood -- with "Glory, Both now"; *Tserkovne Oko* prescribes 10; our Pochaiv and Greek Triodia -- 8, however, inaccurately, for they give only 7, except the two at "Glory, Both now".
[^593]: *Tserkovne Oko*.
[^594]: If on Great Tuesday our *Triodion* gives such, then here also it should be so.
[^595]: New Constantinopolitan Typikon and new Athenian *Triodion*.
[^596]: So in general Slavonic editions; but *Tserkovne Oko* and our Manuscript Typikon prescribe this litany in full, as usual.
[^597]: In the new Constantinopolitan Typikon the Great Dismissal is prescribed, but we have the custom to impart the Great [Dismissal] -- at Great Matins.
[^598]: Latins in the three days of Christ's death not only do not expose the Holy Mysteries, but do not even keep them in the temple; tombs of Christ among them are erected without the Holy Mysteries.
[^599]: According to the rubric of the Greek *Triodion*, our Pochaiv and the Moscow Typikon -- are sung all together at the 2nd hour of the day; according to our Manuscript Typikon, the 1st Hour -- at the 1st hour of the day, and the others -- at the 7th hour of the day. According to *Tserkovne Oko* all -- at the 7th hour of the day; according to the new Constantinopolitan Typikon -- at the 1st hour of the day.
[^600]: The magnificent rite of the Shroud in ancient Triodia and Typika is not given, for it was introduced later; however, today it is used among all followers of the Greek rite, and among us -- also with the exposition of the Holy Mysteries, according to the custom of the Latins of the Austrian State and various German dioceses (Nilles, Calend. T. 2, p. 312). It is described in our Sluzhebnyky, published in Pochaiv back under Stanislaus Augustus in 1767, then in Russian Typika and in the new Typikon of the Patriarchate of Constantinople. However, in our Sluzhebnyky the procession with the Shroud is given only at Vespers, in Russian rubrics -- only at Saturday Matins, after the Great Doxology, and in the Constantinopolitan Typikon the bringing out into the temple to the tomb is prescribed at Vespers, the procession around the temple -- at Matins.
[^601]: Many rubrics add to "The noble Joseph" also the troparion "The angel stood by the tomb" (with the refrain "Glory, Both now"). But *Tserkovne Oko*, our Manuscript Typikon and the Manuscript *Triodion* which we have, give only "The noble Joseph", and so they take in the arch-altar temple.
[^602]: According to the rubric of the new Constantinopolitan Typikon, the placing of the Shroud into the tomb takes place during the singing of the Aposticha, in the following way: "The Aposticha are sung, and six priests with uncovered heads, dressed in priestly vestments, go out from the left door of the sanctuary, carrying with reverence on their heads the Epitaphios /Shroud/, of whom the Archimandrite holds also the Holy Gospel, preceded by singers, the Primicerius holding the Divamboulon (a type of candlestick with two lamps), the Deacons with lamps and censers, and thus proceed up to the prepared canopy, and the singers stand in order, singing the Aposticha, and the Deacons censing go around 3 times with the Priests around the canopy. Then they place the Epitaphios inside the canopy, the doorkeeper sprinkles fragrant flowers upon the Epitaphios, and having approached the Patriarch venerates the Epitaphios, blesses the Christians, and ascends the throne. Then the doorkeeper offers him flowers prepared. Then also the holy hierarchs, two by two, venerating the Epitaphios, receive flowers from the Patriarch, likewise also the Ecclesiastical officials. This being done, the 2nd choir sings the Doxastikon, and from the Doxastikon... Now lettest Thou" and the rest. The description which we have from the island of Corfu gives this: "The icon of the Epitaphios is carried on Holy and Great Friday from the sanctuary at the end of Vespers, while the Dismissal Troparia 'The noble Joseph', etc. are sung, and is placed on a prepared table in the middle of the presbyterium, where there are already and remain lit candles with vessels of flowers throughout the whole day until the hour of Matins of Great Saturday (which is usually celebrated on the evening of Great Friday). Where again at the end of the Great Doxology at 'Holy God', the Epitaphios is carried out, but inside the church and, if circumstances permit, -- outside and again is placed on this same table until the time of the Liturgy of Great Saturday, when one priest privately in an epitrachelion places it in the sanctuary in the usual place".
[^603]: So in our Pochaiv *Triodion*; other editions, from the usual beginning to *“God is the Lord”*, give everything -- as usual, only the Typikon of the Lviv University prescribes beginning from the Six Psalms.
[^604]: Our *Triodion* and the Greek which we have, the Typikon of the Lviv University do not prescribe twice, nevertheless, *Tserkovne Oko*, the Manuscript *Triodion* and Typikon which we have, prescribe twice.
[^605]: In our Pochaiv *Triodion* nothing is prescribed to cense, it is noted only: "and, having censed crosswise". In the Greek *Triodion* censing is mentioned only at the 2nd and 3rd stations and it is not mentioned what should be censed. In *Tserkovne Oko* censing is prescribed at the 1st station of the whole church and brethren according to the order, and at the others -- only of the choirs. In the Constantinopolitan Typikon is prescribed -- only at the 1st station, only of the Shroud and the people: "The Patriarch... censing the Epitaphios, and the whole people".
[^606]: *Tserkovne Oko*.
[^607]: This troparion is prescribed only once: Typikon of Sabbas, Greek *Triodion*, Greek Typikon, our Manuscript Typikon, another of Lviv University; other rubrics prescribe it twice, the second time -- with the refrain "Glory, Both now". *Tserkovne Oko* prescribes it first once, then Glory: the ending, Both now: whole. Obviously, all rubrics have this troparion; and the troparion "The noble Joseph", which is sung before it, is prescribed primarily by various Greek and Slavonic rubrics and the Greek Typikon of Sabbas. The sticheron "Come, let us bless" only our editions have, and the new Constantinopolitan Typikon, before the troparion "The noble Joseph" prescribes also the Resurrection Troparion "When Thou didst descend" and "The angel stood by the tomb". Before the troparion "The noble Joseph" our and Greek rubrics prescribe: "Let us attend. Peace be to all. Wisdom, let us attend", others Slavonic -- only "Wisdom, Aright"; and since they do not prescribe here "The noble Joseph", they prescribe "Wisdom, Aright" to exclaim before the Troparion of the Prophecy. *Tserkovne Oko* prescribes "Wisdom, Aright" before "The noble Joseph", and before the Troparion of the Prophecy: "Let us attend. Peace to Thee. Wisdom, let us attend". The Entrance, according to the Russian rubric, takes place in the following way: "Then the Superior enters the holy altar with the priests and deacons, vests in all sacred vestments, and the priests -- only in phelonia, comes out with the Gospel under the Shroud, with priests who support, and deacons who cense. At this time ringing is done with all might. He is preceded with candles and with two candlesticks, and both choirs sing the funeral Trisagion. The Abbot, having come before the holy royal doors, stands here, awaiting the conclusion of the last Trisagion. When it ends, the Superior with the Gospel enters the royal doors and places the Gospel on the altar, and the Shroud -- on the prepared table, in the form of a tomb. In monasteries, after the dismissal, the kissing of the Shroud, placed in the tomb, takes place". This is -- the Moscow Typikon. In the Patriarchate of Constantinople it takes place thus: "Great Doxology. Then we begin the sung [Trisagion], preceding the Epitaphios, and going out of the temple, the Entrance takes place, as is customary; as soon as we return, the Patriarch enters directly into the holy sanctuary, with the rest, and immediately exclaims 'Let us attend. Peace be to all. Wisdom'. And the Troparion 'When Thou didst descend' is sung. He censes around the holy table, preceded by the Epitaphios, then 'The angel stood by the tomb' up to 'appeared as a stranger'. After this is sung 'The noble Joseph', up to 'wrapped, laid', and they place the Epitaphios on the holy table. At once the canonarch from outside reads the Troparion, the Prophecy and the Apostle, and the Gospel is said by the Patriarch, in front of the Gate" (New Constantinopolitan Typikon). In various parts of Greece, according to the testimony of Allatius, the procession takes place in the following way: "The custom prevailed, that, while Ps. 118 is sung, and at individual verses individual Troparia are sung, Christ beautifully carved, or skillfully painted on a board, and placed in a bier, with a solemn apparatus of burning candles, Priests, dressed as when they celebrate the sacred solemnities of Masses, the rest of the Clergy accompanying not without order, and the faithful of Christ following the bier through the streets of the city, is carried, and set forth to all to be adored, and kissed: and thus is open to the veneration of all. Meanwhile flowers placed on the image, are sought by all with the greatest zeal, which they promise to themselves for the greatest good, not only of the body, but of domestic affairs" (Nil). Kalend. vol. 2, p. 241).
[^608]: According to rubrics: at 10 o'clock in the day; to end the Liturgy -- at the 2nd hour of the night. "At the 2nd hour of the night".

[^610]: So according to the rubric of our and the Russian Triodia; similarly also the Greek Typikon of Sabbas, only, instead of violet, prescribes dark vestments: "The Singer being about to begin the present verse, Arise O God, the priests stand up, take off the black phelonia, and put on white instead of them". According to the Greek *Triodion*, *Tserkovne Oko* and another manuscript rubric, white vestments are prescribed from the beginning of Vespers. Mauros we translate as dark, and not as black, for black will be -- melas.
[^611]: In the new Athenian *Triodion* this service is called Pannychis /Vigil/.
[^612]: 2 Lviv *Sluzhebnik* of 1780 and Moscow Typikon.
[^613]: In Constantinople the Patriarch places the Shroud on the holy table.
[^614]: So it takes place in Russia, according to the testimony of Muralt, letter 14: "around the holy Table, on which the Shroud is spread, which remains here until the Day of the Ascension".
[^615]: According to the ancient rubric of community life the procession goes from the temple into the narthex through the northern doors of this narthex and there, before its central doors leading into the temple, the beginning of Matins is sung. Carried are: Gospel -- by the Priest and censer -- by the Deacon, preceded by candle-bearers, brethren with lit candles, as you have in the Greek *Pentecostarion*. To this the Pochaiv *Triodion* adds the icon of the Resurrection of Christ, and *Tserkovne Oko* -- also the icon of the Most Holy Theotokos and other holy icons, carried by priests and deacons, so that in such a way the procession would be more majestic, than only with candles. According to the custom of the surroundings of Greece, independent of the Patriarch of Constantinople, before this procession the Bishop or priest, standing in the holy doors with a lit candlestick in hand, exclaims in a loud voice: "Come ye, take light from the unwaning light, and glorify Christ, Who is risen from the dead", that is "Come, receive light from the unwaning light and kiss Christ, risen from the dead". And so all approach one by one, to light their candles from him, forming after this the procession (The Holy Passions. Athens. 1892)
[^616]: In the Greek *Triodion* this procession is described thus: "About the hour of Matins all the semantrons sound. And the Ecclesiarch distributes candles to the brethren; the Priest with the Deacon vest in all their priestly attire. Then, taking, the Priest the holy Gospel, and the Deacon the censer, and preceded by lamps, we go out to the narthex, holding lit candles, and singing 'Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior', etc. And in the temple remaining alone the candle-lighter lights all the candles and lamps; and having made a fire, and having put incense into it, places it in the middle of the temple /About the time of Matins all clappers gave notice. The Ecclesiarch distributes candles to the brethren, and the Priest with the Deacon vest in light sacred vestments. Then the Priest, having taken the holy Gospel, and the Deacon -- the censer, preceded by lights, and we all go out to the narthex, holding lit candles and singing: 'Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior'. In the temple remains only the sacristan, who lights all candles and lamps, after which, having lit a fire, throws incense into it and places in the middle of the temple/."
[^617]: Slavonic rubrics before that prescribe to cense everyone, but we, according to the Greek rubric, cense here only directly the church doors. Evidently also our, or Russian rubrics, according to *Tserkovne Oko* prescribe for the Priest to sign with the censer three times crosswise the church doors. The Typikon of the Lviv University orders to cense crosswise, but not three times and not the church doors: "Makes a cross with the censer, saying: 'Glory to the Holy'". The Greek *Pentecostarion* gives only: "and censing says" /and, having censed, exclaims/.
[^618]: So the Greek Typikon of Sabbas, the Typikon of the Lviv University, manuscript Flower Triodia which we have, and our Apostles and Sluzhebnyky. Pochaiv 1788 -- at the Liturgy of Easter, Moscow Typikon -- at Resurrection Matins, other rubrics prescribe three times.
[^619]: According to the new custom of the Greeks, which Slavs do not accept, before the beginning of Matins the Priest sings the Sunday Gospel of Matins, usually -- the 2nd. This the Greek Typikon of Sabbas does not have, but only newly published Greek Pentecostaria. Also according to the custom (and not according to the church rubric) of the Greeks, independent of the Patriarch of Constantinople, the entrance into the church is accompanied by questions and answers taken from the 23rd Psalm: "Lift up your gates, O ye princes, and the King of Glory shall come in" etc. and when is sung: "The Lord of Hosts, He is the King of Glory", the doors are opened and the entrance into the church takes place... "Especially the custom prevailed to enter through question and answer: Lift up gates, and to open the door only at The Lord of powers, He is the King of Glory /Especially the custom prevailed, that the entrance into the church be accompanied by dialogue, question and answer 'Lift up the gates', and the doors are opened only at 'The Lord of Hosts, He is the King of Glory'/, -- is written in the description from Corfu. This custom we meet also among Greek-Melkites, and Italians, and also in various churches of the Latin rite... However, neither in Greek nor in Slavonic rubrics is this met, nor the words of the named psalm fit well here, for according to general explanation they refer not to the descent of Christ into hell, but to His Ascension...
[^620]: "The Priest censes at the beginning of the Canon, according to the order /The Priest censes at the beginning of the canon, as prescribed/ (Greek *Triodion*).
[^621]: That which is prescribed in *Tserkovne Oko* and, following it, in our and the Russian Triodia, that the Small Litany after each ode "will be on this holy day outside the sanctuary", does not agree with the Greek *Triodion*, for in it, instead of "outside the sanctuary", is given "inside the sanctuary",... as have also the Typikon of the Lviv University and the manuscript Slavonic *Triodion* which we have. However, this contradiction can be eliminated if we say that the Greek *Triodion* and other rubrics order on this day to sing all litanies for the Priest, and not for the Deacon, and for the Deacon -- only to carry the censer and recite the verses "Let God arise"; and with this assumption the Priest sings all litanies inside the sanctuary, at the holy table... "At each Ode takes place by the Priest, inside the Sanctuary, a Small Litany /At each ode by the Priest, inside the sanctuary, is sung a Small Litany/, -- is written in the *Triodion*, which also other litanies prescribes to the Priest. Finally, "inside" and "outside", differ only by one letter, therefore we see that copyists could easily make a mistake.
[^622]: According to the rubric of the Greek *Triodion* the kissing takes place thus: "The Priest takes the holy Gospel, and stands before the doors of the holy Sanctuary but the Superior having come, and having kissed the holy Gospel, and the Priest, receives it from his hands, and stands on the right of the Priest. Then the Brethren all, according to their order, kiss first the holy Gospel, then the Priest and the Superior, and stand also there where they happen to be, and kiss one another /The Priest takes the Holy Gospel and stands before the doors of the sanctuary. And the Abbot, having come and kissed the Gospel and the Priest, takes it from his hands and stands on the right side of the Priest. Then all brethren, according to their rank, kiss first the Gospel, and then -- the Priest and the Abbot, and stand there, where possible, kissing mutually/. According to the rubrics of our Pochaiv, Russian Triodia, *Tserkovne Oko* and our Manuscript Typikon, the kissing first takes place in the sanctuary between the sacred ministers, then -- in the church, before the iconostasis, between clerics and elders, and at the end -- between the faithful and sacred ministers and between themselves. This is -- the rubric: "The kissing of the Superior with other priests and deacons in the holy altar takes place in this way: He who approaches says: 'Christ is risen', and he answers: 'Truly He is risen' and they kiss. Then the Superior, having taken the cross, stands outside before the holy royal doors, also all priests, as many as there be, and deacons, having taken each the Gospel and holy icons, according to their rank, stand in a row to the right of the Superior. Approach first the most worthy clerics and elders, one by one, and, bowing slightly before the Superior, kiss each the precious cross and Gospel which the Priest and images hold, and the Superior himself on the mouth, saying: 'Christ is risen', and he answers: 'Truly He is risen'. In such a way they kiss also the priests, and they themselves, in order, kiss among themselves, standing in a row to the right of the priests. After them similarly kiss also the faithful" (Moscow Typikon and Pochaiv *Triodion* 1786).
[^623]: The Synod of Lviv here, on [p. 21](Final_Dolnytsky_part1_structure.md#order-of-great-vespers-without-vigil), in the notes.
[^624]: So in our Sluzhebnyky, but in our and Russian Triodia is not prescribed "Shine", instead of "More honorable", nor, instead of "Glory to Thee, O Christ God, our hope", -- "Christ is risen" up to "trampling down death by death", with the response: "and upon those in the tombs bestowing life". Greek rubrics do not prescribe anything of this, nor the dismissal with the cross, but prescribe the dismissal "Who rose from the dead", as on Sunday (Roman *Euchologion* 1873, p. 79).
[^625]: Compare the rubric of the Sunday of Ap. Thomas in the evening with the rubric of Small Vespers of the Ascension of the Lord. About this also in the new Typikon of the Patriarchate of Constantinople is written: "Many also after the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, ignoring, invoke the O Heavenly King Comforter, etc. in which this is not pardoned, our Savior being still on earth, except from the 1st of the Ascension, or from the first Pentecost, because at the third hour of this day descended the Holy Spirit... as from this therefore the invocation of the Comforter Spirit took beginning, from this day, which ceases from the day of the Resurrection until Pentecost. (On Monday of the Holy Spirit) /Many not considering, also after the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, read 'O Heavenly King, Comforter' etc., which -- is inadmissible, when our Savior will still be on earth until the first hour of the Ascension, or until the first hour of Pentecost, for at the third hour of this day descended the Holy Spirit... as, finally, from this began to invoke the Holy Spirit the Comforter, from that day, which ceases from the day of the Resurrection until Pentecost (On Monday of the Holy Spirit)/.
[^626]: So about "Christ is risen" in our Sluzhebnyky, except "We have seen", and in its place they have "Christ is risen", however, such is our custom and so in the Pochaiv *Triodion* of 1786... and in the Moscow Typikon of 1859... Ancient Greek rubrics prescribe "Christ is risen" only instead of "Blessed be the name" and instead of the psalm "I will bless the Lord", as in the Slavonic Typikon of the Lviv University. A later custom of the Greeks -- to sing "Christ is risen" after "Blessed is the Kingdom" three times and, instead of "We have seen the true light" and instead of "Blessed be the name of the Lord", -- three times. However, some of them, after "Blessed is the Kingdom" sing "Christ is risen" with its verses, as is given at the beginning of Resurrection Matins. The Moscow Typikon follows them, but the new Constantinopolitan Typikon does not go. What we said about the custom of the Greeks, we took from a description which we have from the island of Corfu, in which is written the following: "After 'Blessed is the kingdom' the Priest 'Christ is risen', and successively repeat it, first the right followed by the left choir; and this happens on all the days of Pascha until the Ascension. But on the great Sunday, and on those of the New Week we follow to sing it after its verses unchanged; as was said previously at Matins... Is sung successively 'Christ is risen' – as much on the great Sunday as on the remaining days of Pascha at 'With fear' instead of 'We have seen the light', and before the Dismissal three times flowingly instead of 'Blessed be the name', and at the end, at the Dismissal instead of 'Through the prayers' /After 'Blessed is the Kingdom' the Priest: 'Christ is risen', successively again repeat it: first -- the right, then -- and the left choir. And so it will be on all days from the Resurrection to the Ascension. But on the Great Sunday and on the days of Bright Week we continue to sing invariable this with its verses, as is taken at Matins... Successively is sung 'Christ is risen' on the Great Sunday as much as on the rest of the days of the Resurrection: at 'With fear', instead of 'We have seen the light' and before the dismissal three times flowingly, instead of 'Blessed be the name' and at the end, at the dismissal, instead of 'Through the prayers of our holy fathers'/.

[^628]: "Then is read the Holy Gospel by the Patriarch, and by the holy High Priests (periodically in different dialects, as is customary) /Then is read the Holy Gospel by the Patriarch and by other hierarchs (by turn, in different languages, as is customary)/. New Constantinopolitan Typikon, on the day of Resurrection at Vespers.
[^629]: Or, as in the *Triodion* -- after the dismissal of the Liturgy.
[^630]: In the Rite of the Panagia, given in the *Horologion* before or after the 9th Hour, it is recounted how the apostles after Christ's Resurrection, before the dispersion throughout the whole world, stayed together in Jerusalem, having the custom to dine together and at this time to leave at the table an empty place, on which they placed a pillow, and on it -- : a piece of bread in Christ's portion, that is in memory of Jesus Christ, and after dinner they elevated the piece, saying: "Glory to Thee, O Christ God, help us"; from the Resurrection to the Ascension: "Christ is risen". When the apostles did this after the Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos, she appeared to them in the air alive, in light radiance, surrounded by angels, saying: "Rejoice, for I am with you all days". And they frightened, instead of "Glory to Thee, O Christ God", exclaimed "All-holy (Panagia) Theotokos, help us". This rite of the Panagia, named so from the name Panagia /All-holy/, by which the apostles invoked then the Most Holy Theotokos, imitating the apostles, was repeated once by the Emperor in the Court... and by people in churches or homes, and predominantly daily in monasteries, as is seen from the service of the meal, given in the *Horologion*, however, more solemnly -- in Bright Week, in which not a piece of bread, which they ate, but a whole (whole) bread they offered on all days of the week, not eating until Bright Saturday, but only kissing it. And this rite was initially served only at the meal, as it is in the Greek *Pentecostarion*. The Slavs, for the sake of greater solemnity, did not serve the whole rite only at the meal, but daily, throughout the whole Bright Week, preceded by lights and the icon of the Resurrection carried the Artos from the church to the meal and from the meal to the church, to the sounds of bells, as for *Tserkovne Oko* has our Pochaiv *Triodion* and Russian Typika. Today this rite is celebrated among us only in Bright Week and not with all prayers and rites, as the *Triodion* gives, but only as here, in the text, we gave, however, not only in monasteries, but also in all other churches. The prayers for the blessing and breaking of the Artos the Slavs added to themselves, for in Greek books they are not encountered; the prayer for breaking is not given even in Slavonic rubrics, except ours, but others break it without prayer.
[^631]: If a Bishop serves, we consider that he should begin Vespers in the sanctuary, censing before the holy table and from there read the verses, after which depart to his throne. And at "O Gladsome Light", after the blessing with the di- and trikirion he enters the sanctuary and from the holy doors reads the Gospel, after which returns to his throne.
[^632]: Some consider (among them also the new Typikon of the Patriarchate of Constantinople) that throughout the whole Bright Week Vespers should begin not from "Blessed is our God", but from "Glory to the Holy", as Matins. However, they are mistaken, for in all editions which we have, is indicated clearly "Blessed is our God": "Blessed is our God"... and the Greek Typikon of Sabbas: "Signs crosswise with the censer, saying: 'Blessed is our God'" (On the Sunday of the Resurrection, at Vespers).
[^633]: The previous rubric at Vespers of Monday evening and other days of Bright Week is silent about sacred vestments. At the beginning, after Matins, in the *Pentecostarion*: "without however the priestly robe /probably without the priestly chasuble/; and the Typikon of the Lviv University, our Manuscript and Moscow Typika -- exactly so; similarly also our Pochaiv *Triodion* of 1786, however, adds: "or which is the custom where" and "in secular temples the Priest vests in vestments", that is in the phelonion. *Tserkovne Oko* prescribes also the phelonion.
[^634]: Regarding censing, our *Triodion* and the Moscow Typikon do not mention here any censing. "It is necessary to know, that after the Priest blesses, while 'Christ is risen' is sung, he censes the holy Table, as usual, and all the Priesthood; at the beginning of the Canon he goes out, and censes the Temple, and the brothers, according to the accustomed order".
